newsitem.title: LATVIA: FEATURE - Baltic states -- eastern Europe's Hong Kong?.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Baltic states -- eastern Europe's Hong Kong?.

text.p: The Baltic states of Latvia, Estonia and Lithuania, in the throes of recovering from 50 years of communism, seem far removed from the bustle and buzz of skyscraper-packed Hong Kong.
Improvements are being made but five years after the three quit the former Soviet Union, the infrastructure creaks, roads are often potholed and many buildings are rundown.

Some analysts, however, have high hopes for them and say they could be for eastern Europe what Hong Kong is in Asia: a transit gateway for a huge neighbour, in this case Russia, and even high-tech, export-oriented manufacturers.
BALTICS SEEN AS FASTEST AND MOST CONVINCED REFORMERS
The Baltic states are credited with being the fastest and most convinced reformers of the former Soviet countries.
"I am not 100 percent convinced they will become like Hong Kong but I think there is that potential," Lino Lourenco, an economist at securities house Daiwa, told Reuters.
Such ambitions may be some way off but both Latvia and Estonia are already pushing themselves as bridges between Russia and the West, given their port and rail facilities.
They are also hoping to benefit from Scandinavian investment as the Nordic states' interest in their neighbours on the other side of the Baltic Sea is rekindled.

Latvia and Estonia would be recapturing a past when the two were thriving commercial centres with Hanseatic ports, centuries before 50 years as unwilling Soviet republics knit them tightly into the communist-bloc trading system.
Latvia has the biggest port on the Baltic Sea at its western city of Ventspils. The oil terminal there is one of the main outlets for Russian crude.
In 1995, Ventspils had cargo turnover of 29 million tonnes, compared with 22 million in Gdansk and 10.5 million in St Petersburg. Fourth-placed was Estonia's port of Tallinn at 13 million tonnes.

"I have always regarded Estonia not only as a potential Hong Hong but say that should be its main strategy for the future," said Basil Zavoico, Estonia's International Monetary Fund (IMF) resident representative.
ESTONIA CONSIDERED MOST ECONOMICALLY ADVANCED
Estonia is already considered by many Western investors as the most economically advanced of the three Baltic states, with an open economy and advanced privatisation programme.
Tallinn, the capital, also seems less rundown than those of Latvia and Lithuania.
But Zavoico said the key step of creating a truly free land market was needed if Estonia was to fulfill its potential and attract the kind of investment that would make it a Hong Kong.
The first glimmers of such investment are there, with plans by U.S. computer giant Western Digital WCD.N to set up a hard-drive repair centre for eastern Europe in Estonia.
Finnish computer maker Elcoteq Network Oy is also expanding its plant there.
LATVIA HAS BEST TRANSIT POTENTIAL, ANALYSTS SAY
Latvia, hit last year by a severe banking crisis, has with Ventspils and Riga port the best transit potential of the three Baltic states, analysts say.
It has also set its sights on being an offshore banking centre for Russians although the banking crisis hit those hopes.
But Latvia has not so far attracted the kind of investment Hong Kong draws.

"There are many things here that are not like Hong Kong. The latter is prepared to accept investment from anywhere in the world with no restrictions," said one senior Western financial official based in Latvia.
He said Latvia needed to free its highly-restricted land market and create a better legal and bureaucratic framework.
Analysts said problems were bound to arise when countries were recreating themselves and adapting to a new system after 50 years of communism.
"You cannot rebuild a country overnight and you have to assign priorities," said the IMF's Zavoico.
Lithuania, with only the port of Klaipeda as a transit facility, seems to have less of a claim as a Baltic Hong Kong.

The southernmost of the Baltic states has also been branded the most reluctant reformer, given a slow pace of privatisation and the fact that most key state-owned companies such as telecommunications and airlines are to stay in government hands.
Officials argue with this characterisation and point out that Lithuania cooperates well with Western banks and has changed laws so foreigners can own land for commercial use.

Algis Avizhienis, head of the Lithuanian Investment Agency said Lithuania had ambitions to be a transport hub for eastern Europe, given Klaipeda, and plans for a large cargo airport near the northern city of Siauliai.
It has also encouraged regional investment with free economic zones that give tax breaks for investors.
He said Lithuania had prospects for exports and investments in the textile sector, fertilisers and television equipment.
"Being a Hong Kong is something that we could aspire to," Avizhienis said.
